# `yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans`

**No yes/no/on/off as unquoted values**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pack** | `@codelaw/rules-data` (npm) · `codelaw-rules-data` (PyPI) |
| **Languages** | YAML |
| **Turned on by** | `codelaw:data/recommended` at `warn` |
| **Severity when named without one** | `error` |
| **Options** | none — severity only |
| **Fix** | `suggest` — `codelaw fix --unsafe` applies it; review the diff, it can change behaviour (quoting keeps the YAML 1.2 meaning (a string); if a boolean was meant, write `true` or `false` instead) |
| **Stability** | `preview` — runs only with `preview = true` |
| **Since** | 0.1.0 |

## What it checks

A value is not a bare `yes`, `no`, `on` or `off` (in any of their capitalisations). Quote it if it is text, or write `true` or `false` if it is a boolean. Keys are not checked, so a GitHub Actions `on:` is fine.

**Why:** YAML 1.2 reads these words as strings, but YAML 1.1 loaders, still common (PyYAML, Ruby's Psych, many tools built on them), read them as booleans: `country: no` becomes `false`.

## Configuration

Everything below goes in `codelaw.toml` at the repo root. The same keys work as `[tool.codelaw]` in `pyproject.toml` or `"codelaw"` in `package.json` ([SR-CONFIG](../../../records/0110_config.md)).

### Turn it on

**Install the pack** (`codelaw init` does it for the languages it finds):

```bash
npm install --save-dev @codelaw/rules-data
pip install codelaw-rules-data
```

**Then extend a preset that turns it on** — `codelaw:data/recommended` sets it to `warn`:

```toml
preview = true                        # pack rules are preview today
extends = ["codelaw:data/recommended"]
```

- **A rule exists only once its pack is loaded** through `extends`; naming it in `[rules]` without that is an unknown rule id (exit 2).
- **Without `preview = true`** the rule is skipped and codelaw warns that it is preview.

### Severity

```toml
[rules]
"yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans" = "warn"    # error | warn | info | off
```

- **`error`** fails the run (exit 1) · **`warn`** fails only with `--max-warnings N` · **`info`** never fails · **`off`** turns it off.
- **Naming it with a severity turns it on** even when no preset does.

### For a group of files

A `[scope.<name>]` gives some files their own setting, applied after `[rules]` — a scope of your own needs `files`:

```toml
[scope.legacy]
files = ["src/legacy/**/*.yaml"]
rules = { "yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans" = "off" }
```

A scope's `remap` changes whole severities in its files, after everything else: `remap = { error = "warn" }` never fails the run there.

### Warn locally, fail in CI

The `ci` profile runs when `CI` is set; `local` otherwise; `--profile <name>` or `CODELAW_PROFILE` picks one.

```toml
[profile.local.rules]
"yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans" = "warn"

[profile.ci.rules]
"yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans" = "error"
```

### In `pyproject.toml` or `package.json`

```toml
# pyproject.toml
[tool.codelaw.rules]
"yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans" = { severity = "warn" }
```

```json
{
  "codelaw": {
    "rules": {
      "yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans": {"severity": "warn"}
    }
  }
}
```

### Silence one finding

An inline `codelaw-ignore` always needs a reason; `expires=`, `warn_days=` and `by=` date it ([SR-LINTER](../../../records/0106_linter.md) decision 6).

- **YAML:** `# codelaw-ignore yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans: <reason>`
- **Dated:** `# codelaw-ignore yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans expires=2026-12-31 by=you@example.com: <reason>`

### Keep today's findings, fail on new ones

```bash
codelaw baseline add --rule yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans --expires 2026-12-31 --reason "<why>"
```

See [SR-BASELINE](../../../records/0104_baseline-and-deprecations.md).

### See what applies

```bash
codelaw explain yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans       # what it wants, why, how to fix
codelaw check --rule yaml/no-ambiguous-booleans  # only this rule
codelaw config --print --for <file>              # the resolved setting, and where it came from
```

## Examples

### YAML

#### Don't

```yaml
country: no
```

#### Do

```yaml
country: "no"
```

#### Do

```yaml
enabled: true
```

## Differences from the source

The idea comes from the YAML 1.1 and 1.2 specifications. `y` and `n` are not reported: the YAML 1.1 type repository lists them, but the common 1.1 loaders don't treat them as booleans.
